strengths: Addresses a genuine practical gap: prior feed-forward language-Gaussian methods are restricted to a fixed, typically very small number of views (often just 2) or require known camera parameters, whereas FLEG operates as a single model across a wide range of view counts (2 to 32+) without calibration.

The 3D-annotation-free training framework, which leverages a pretrained geometric foundation model (VGGT) for pseudo geometric supervision plus a novel-view coverage-mask selection mechanism for photometric supervision, is a sensible and well-motivated way to sidestep the scarcity of posed 3D training data.

Construction of InstanceMV-14K, a large-scale (15M+ images, ~14K scenes) multi-view dataset with instance masks drawn from both annotated scans and Internet video via SAM2, is a useful resource-level contribution that could benefit the community beyond this paper.

The instance-guided contrastive learning is a reasonable, computationally cheaper (O(N_p K) vs O(N_p^2)) alternative to dense pixel-wise contrastive objectives, and the geometry-semantic hierarchical sparsification (decoupling sparse isotropic semantic Gaussians from denser geometry Gaussians) is a sound engineering idea for controlling memory/compute overhead under dense-view semantic embedding.

Empirical results are consistently strong: FLEG outperforms feed-forward baselines (LSM, Uni3R, LSeg) across all tested view counts on both NVS metrics and open-vocabulary segmentation, and remains stable as view count grows while baselines degrade sharply; it also beats per-scene optimized methods (LangSplat, LangScene-X) in accuracy while being orders of magnitude faster (seconds vs. 10-20 minutes).
Ablations (Table 3) meaningfully isolate the contribution of the distillation loss, instance contrastive loss, and sparsification, supporting the design choices.
weaknesses: The 'annotation-free' framing is somewhat overstated: the pipeline still critically depends on outputs (point maps, camera poses) from a pretrained 3D foundation model (VGGT) as pseudo-labels, so errors or biases in VGGT's predictions directly propagate into FLEG's supervision; this dependency and any resulting error analysis (e.g., sensitivity to VGGT's failure modes) is not discussed.

Evaluation is restricted to indoor scene datasets (ScanNet, ScanNet++); no results are shown on outdoor or more diverse/unconstrained scenes despite the dataset including Internet video (RealEstate10K) and claims of 'any views' generality.

The 3D editing capability, prominently shown in Figure 1 as a headline application, is never described in the methodology and has no quantitative or even further qualitative evaluation in the experiments section, leaving its mechanism and reliability unclear.

Fairness of baseline comparisons could be scrutinized further: fixed-view baselines (LSM, Uni3R) are adapted to multi-view settings via a DUSt3R-style post-processing strategy not originally designed for them, which may understate their true achievable performance and make the comparison somewhat asymmetric in FLEG's favor.

No explicit limitations or failure-case discussion is provided (e.g., behavior under extremely sparse or extremely dense/occluded inputs, sensitivity to VGGT pseudo-label noise, or generalization to unseen semantic categories/domains), which would strengthen the credibility of the claims.

Key hyperparameters (voxel sizes ϵ_geo/ϵ_sem, coverage threshold τ, temperature α) are introduced but not ablated for sensitivity, leaving the robustness of the sparsification and view-selection strategies to different scene scales/densities unverified.
Training cost/resources for the ~1B-parameter model on a 15M-image dataset are not reported, which affects reproducibility and practical assessment of the method's accessibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely useful and underexplored problem: a single feed-forward model that handles both sparse and dense, uncalibrated/unposed views for language-embedded Gaussian reconstruction, unlike prior two-view-only or pose-dependent methods.

The 3D-annotation-free training framework via distillation from VGGT pseudo-labels and novel-view photometric supervision is a sensible way to avoid costly 3D ground truth while still enabling cross-view consistent supervision.

The construction of InstanceMV-14K, leveraging existing scan datasets and SAM2-derived instance masks on Internet video, is a reasonably large-scale and practically useful resource for training feed-forward semantic Gaussians.

The geometry-semantic hierarchical sparsification strategy that decouples geometry and semantic voxel densities, including the isotropic covariance approximation for sparse semantic Gaussians, is a reasonable and seemingly novel engineering contribution to reduce memory/compute overhead.

Quantitative results show consistent and fairly large improvements over feed-forward baselines (LSM, Uni3R) across 2/8/16/32-view settings in both NVS and segmentation metrics, and the method is shown to be much faster than per-scene optimized baselines while achieving better open-vocabulary query accuracy.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: LSM and Uni3R are designed for fixed/limited views, and the paper applies an undefined 'post-processing strategy following DUSt3R' to adapt them to multi-view settings without detailing how this is done, which could bias results in FLEG's favor; no comparison is given against more recent or stronger feed-forward multi-view baselines (e.g., AnySplat, which is cited and conceptually very related, or SpatialSplat, SemanticSplat, UniForward) despite these being directly relevant competitors explicitly discussed in related work.

The core architecture is a fairly direct extension of VGGT with added Gaussian/semantic heads initialized from pretrained VGGT weights; much of the novelty rests on training strategy (distillation, novel-view masking) and sparsification rather than a fundamentally new architecture, and the degree of architectural originality beyond combining known components (VGGT backbone + DPT Gaussian head + CLIP distillation + contrastive loss) is limited.

The reliance on VGGT pseudo-labels as geometric supervision means the method's geometric accuracy is fundamentally upper-bounded by VGGT's own prediction quality (which can itself be noisy, especially in less-constrained Internet video like RealEstate10K), yet no analysis of pseudo-label noise, failure cases, or error propagation is provided.

Evaluation is limited to ScanNet and ScanNet++, both indoor scene datasets; no evaluation on outdoor, object-centric, or more diverse real-world scenes is shown despite the paper claiming generalization from 'any views' including Internet video data (RealEstate10K) used in training—this leaves open whether the model generalizes well to the diverse data it was trained on or only to indoor benchmarks resembling ScanNet.

No reported variance/multiple seeds, no discussion of failure cases or qualitative limitations (e.g., when sparsification harms thin structures or small objects), and no analysis of sensitivity to the various hyperparameters (voxel sizes, coverage threshold τ, loss weights) that were seemingly tuned without ablation.

The ablation study (Table 3) is relatively shallow: it only tests two global ablations each for reconstruction and language modules (w/o distill loss, w/o inst loss, w/o sparse), without isolating individual contributions like the novel-view photometric loss, the 3D feature aggregation module, or the isotropic approximation specifically versus plain voxel averaging, making it hard to attribute gains to specific proposed components.

Memory/compute efficiency claims (e.g., inference times of 1.89s/3.20s) are not accompanied by GPU memory usage comparisons or a breakdown of how much the hierarchical sparsification specifically saves in FLOPs/memory versus the vanilla pixel-wise approach, despite this being framed as a key contribution.

The CLIP feature aggregation and instance-guided contrastive learning rely heavily on the quality of SAM2-derived masks for in-the-wild video, which can be noisy or inconsistent in dynamic/Internet video, and there's no quantitative assessment of mask quality or its effect on the resulting semantic embeddings.

Reproducibility is a concern given the dataset (InstanceMV-14K) and model (~1B parameters) are large-scale and no code, data, or pretrained weights release statement is explicitly confirmed in the text (project page is referenced but left blank in the abstract).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important limitation of prior feed-forward language-embedded Gaussian methods, namely fixed/limited input view counts and reliance on costly 3D annotations, by proposing a single model that handles arbitrary uncalibrated, unposed views from sparse to dense.

The 3D-annotation-free training framework is a clever technical contribution: using a pretrained geometric foundation model (VGGT) to generate coverage masks and select novel target views enables photometric supervision for cross-view consistency without any ground-truth 3D annotations, which is a reasonable way to bootstrap training from 2D video data.

Construction of InstanceMV-14K, a large-scale (15M+ images, ~14K scenes) multi-view dataset with instance masks aggregated from multiple existing sources, is a solid engineering contribution that could benefit the community if released.

The instance-guided contrastive learning is well justified both for improving semantic discriminability and for its favorable computational complexity (O(N_p K) vs. O(N_p^2)) relative to standard pixel-wise contrastive learning.

The geometry-semantic hierarchical sparsification strategy is a sensible design that exploits the differing spatial density needs of geometry vs. semantics, with a principled covariance-fusion/isotropic-approximation derivation.

Extensive and fairly comprehensive experiments: comparisons against feed-forward baselines (LSM, Uni3R, LSeg) across 2/8/16/32 views show consistent superiority and notably more stable performance as view count increases (where baselines degrade sharply), and comparisons against per-scene optimization methods (LangSplat, LangScene-X) show large efficiency gains (seconds vs. 10-20 minutes) alongside better open-vocabulary query accuracy.
Ablation studies support the necessity of key components (distillation loss, instance loss, sparsification) and quantify their effect on both quality metrics and embedding memory footprint.
weaknesses: The method's geometric quality is fundamentally upper-bounded by the pretrained VGGT teacher used for distillation; the paper does not analyze failure cases where VGGT pseudo-labels are inaccurate (e.g., in textureless or dynamic regions) or how such errors propagate to the final Gaussian reconstruction and semantics.

Pseudo-label quality for non-scan datasets (e.g., RealEstate10K) relies on SAM2-generated instance masks without any validation or noise analysis; the impact of imperfect segmentation on the CLIP-feature distillation and contrastive learning is not studied.

Evaluation is restricted to indoor scene datasets (ScanNet, ScanNet++); no experiments demonstrate generalization to outdoor scenes, object-centric captures, or other domains despite the claim of handling 'any views.'

No explicit runtime/memory comparison against the other feed-forward baselines (LSM, Uni3R) is reported (only against per-scene optimization methods), making it hard to judge FLEG's actual efficiency advantage over comparably fast feed-forward competitors, especially given the ~1B parameter model size.
The 3D editing capability highlighted in Figure 1 is only shown qualitatively with no quantitative evaluation or comparison to editing baselines.

The paper lacks an explicit discussion of limitations or failure modes (e.g., very large scenes, extreme sparse-view degenerate cases, or scenes with rare/ambiguous instance semantics), which would strengthen the honesty and completeness of the claims.

Some architectural/training choices (e.g., novel-view coverage threshold τ, voxel sizes ϵ_geo and ϵ_sem) are not ablated, leaving their sensitivity and the robustness of the chosen hyperparameters unclear.

strengths: Addresses a clear practical gap in feed-forward language-embedded Gaussian Splatting: prior methods are restricted to fixed/small numbers of views or require camera parameters, while this method supports arbitrary uncalibrated views in a single feed-forward pass.

The core empirical finding—that semantic representations are far sparser than geometric ones—is well-supported by a dedicated sensitivity analysis (Fig. 5) showing that increasing vsem drastically cuts storage/embedding count with minimal mIoU degradation until a clear breakpoint, lending credibility to the DGLE design.

Extensive and carefully constructed experimental suite: comparisons across 2/4/8/16/32 input views, cross-dataset generalization to the unseen Replica dataset, ablations isolating each proposed component (novel-view distillation, contrastive loss, sparse vs. dense semantic embeddings), and additional camera-pose and depth-estimation comparisons against VGGT/AnySplat in the supplementary material.

The dual-branch distillation framework enables training without 3D ground truth or semantic labels, which is a practically valuable property for scaling training data, and the paper demonstrates this claim is exercised through the use of off-the-shelf SAM2/CLIP supervision.

Storage reduction is substantial and clearly quantified (~5% of embeddings, ~20x less storage) while maintaining or improving semantic fidelity relative to dense per-Gaussian embedding baselines, which is the paper's central practical contribution.
Reasonably thorough qualitative results (novel-view synthesis, open-vocabulary segmentation, 3D language field visualizations) across multiple datasets support the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: The overall pipeline is largely a combination/extension of existing components (VGGT backbone and distillation, AnySplat-style voxelization, SAM2+CLIP instance supervision, standard contrastive learning), so the core technical novelty is somewhat incremental; the main new ideas are the novel-view selection heuristic and the two-tier (geometric vs. semantic) voxelization scheme, which, while effective, are conceptually straightforward extensions.

Geometric quality is fundamentally upper-bounded by the frozen VGGT teacher, which the paper acknowledges, but this raises questions about how much of the reconstruction quality gain over baselines stems from better VGGT-based initialization versus the proposed contributions.

Comparisons with LSM and Uni3R at higher view counts use their officially released two-view models applied to nearest-neighbor view pairs rather than any retrained multi-view variant; while the authors justify this and cite precedent, it may still understate the achievable performance of these baselines under denser inputs, making the sparse/dense-view comparisons somewhat asymmetric.

Evaluation is restricted entirely to indoor scenes (ScanNet, ScanNet++, Replica); no outdoor or more diverse domain evaluation is provided, so claims of general applicability to "arbitrary views" and broad practical deployment remain untested outside this narrow domain.

The paper does not report inference-time latency/throughput or GPU memory comparisons against baselines (only training resource comparability is mentioned), which is important for a method whose central claimed advantage is real-time/feed-forward practicality.

The instance-guided contrastive loss and CLIP-feature alignment, while shown useful via ablation, are conceptually similar to existing distillation contrastive setups in prior open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian works; the specific complexity argument (O(NpK) vs O(Np^2)) is a reasonable but relatively minor algorithmic contribution.

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical gap: prior feed-forward language-embedded Gaussian methods are restricted to two views or require camera poses; FLEG supports arbitrary, unposed, variable-count inputs (2-32+ views) in a single model.

The observation that semantic signal is much sparser than geometric signal is a reasonable and practically useful insight, and the resulting DGLE compact semantic representation achieves a large (~20x) reduction in storage with comparable mIoU/mAcc, which is a concrete, measurable contribution.

Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple datasets (ScanNet, ScanNet++, and out-of-distribution Replica), multiple view counts, both NVS metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) and open-vocabulary segmentation metrics (mIoU/mAcc), plus supplementary pose-estimation and depth-estimation comparisons against VGGT/AnySplat.

Ablations (Table 3, Fig. 5) reasonably isolate the contributions of the sparse semantic representation, instance-guided contrastive loss, and novel-view distillation, supporting the claimed design choices.

Training pipeline avoids costly 3D/semantic ground truth by distilling from off-the-shelf foundation models (VGGT, CLIP, SAM2), which is a practical and scalable strategy, and the paper is transparent about this design and its limitations.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is incremental: the backbone is essentially VGGT with an added Gaussian head, geometric supervision is pseudo-labels distilled from a frozen VGGT, and the voxelization-based Gaussian compaction closely follows AnySplat; the main novel elements (novel-view selection via coverage masks, instance-contrastive CLIP distillation, and the isotropic-covariance DGLE fusion) are relatively simple extensions of existing ideas rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.

The baseline comparison protocol for LSM and Uni3R (restricting them to their official 2-view pretrained checkpoints and feeding only the two nearest views regardless of the total input-view count) likely disadvantages these methods at higher view counts (8/16/32 views) and may overstate FLEG's relative advantage in those settings; Uni3R is also described inconsistently (claimed to "extend to multi-view settings" in related work but then only evaluated with a 2-view protocol).

No reported inference-time or memory/runtime benchmarks for the proposed feed-forward model despite motivating the work by contrasting with slow per-scene optimization; without such numbers the practicality/real-time claims are not directly substantiated.

Generalization is only demonstrated across indoor scenes (ScanNet, ScanNet++, Replica); despite claiming the training pipeline could scale to arbitrary video data, no outdoor or more diverse domain evaluation is provided, so the breadth of the generalization claim is not fully supported.

Quantitative comparisons omit several directly relevant recent concurrent feed-forward semantic reconstruction methods mentioned in related work (e.g., SemanticSplat, SpatialSplat, UniForward, IGGT), which would strengthen the claim of state-of-the-art performance.

The isotropic approximation and voxel-size hyperparameter (v_sem) for semantic Gaussians are justified mainly empirically (Fig. 5) without deeper analysis of failure cases, e.g., how small or thin objects are affected by coarse semantic voxelization, which is relevant given the open-vocabulary query use case.

Minor presentation issues: project page link is empty, dense/overloaded notation in the method section, and some ablation results (e.g., mIoU/mAcc increasing slightly without sparsity in Table 3, row 2) are not fully explained.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: feed-forward language-embedded Gaussian reconstruction that supports arbitrary numbers of uncalibrated/unposed views in a single model, overcoming the two-view or pose-dependent limitations of prior feed-forward semantic Gaussian methods (LSM, Uni3R, SemanticSplat, etc.).

The dual-branch distillation framework is a sound and practical way to avoid costly 3D/semantic ground truth, leveraging VGGT for geometry and CLIP/SAM2 for semantics, enabling training on arbitrary video/multi-view collections without manual annotation.

The novel-view-based distillation strategy is a clear and well-justified design choice to reduce overfitting to input views; the ablation (Table 3, line 5) and the pose/depth comparisons in the supplementary (Tables 4-5) convincingly show reduced input-view overfitting relative to AnySplat.

The core empirical observation that semantic representations are much sparser than geometric ones is interesting and well substantiated by the DGLE ablation (Table 3) and the systematic voxel-size sweep in the supplementary (Fig. 5), showing a >20x storage reduction with comparable mIoU/mAcc.

Extensive experimentation: comparisons across 2/4/8/16/32 input views, two indoor datasets plus a held-out generalization dataset (Replica), reconstruction and semantic metrics, qualitative results, and multiple supplementary analyses (pose accuracy, depth accuracy, semantic sparsity sweep) that substantially strengthen the empirical case beyond the main tables.

Consistent and often large improvements over relevant feed-forward and per-scene-optimized baselines across nearly all settings and metrics, suggesting the gains are not cherry-picked to a narrow setting.

Reasonable reproducibility: implementation details, hyperparameters, and training data/compute are specified, and baselines are evaluated with official code/checkpoints under a clearly described (if imperfect) protocol.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined entirely to indoor scenes (ScanNet, ScanNet++, Replica); no outdoor or more heterogeneous data is tested, so claims of general 'any views' applicability are only demonstrated within a narrow domain, a limitation the authors acknowledge but that meaningfully bounds the significance of the contribution.

The comparison protocol for LSM and Uni3R (using their 2-view pretrained models with nearest-view selection even under 8/16-view settings) is a reasonable workaround but still an imperfect apples-to-apples comparison, since these baselines are not retrained for the multi-view regime that FLEG is designed for; the resulting large performance gaps should be interpreted with this caveat in mind.

The method's core geometric quality is fundamentally capped by the frozen VGGT teacher (acknowledged in Limitations); as VGGT itself is imperfect, especially for wide-baseline or dynamic scenes, this ceiling could limit real-world applicability beyond curated indoor datasets.

Memory/storage scaling with very large numbers of input views (hundreds/thousands) is unaddressed beyond a note in the limitations section, which somewhat undercuts the 'any views' framing for genuinely large-scale scenarios relevant to the claimed embodied/AR applications.

Some technical exposition (e.g., precise derivation and justification of the isotropic covariance approximation in DGLE, or the interaction between voxelized standard Gaussians and semantic Gaussians during rendering) is fairly dense and could benefit from clearer illustration to aid reproducibility of the DGLE module specifically.

Comparisons with per-scene-optimized baselines (LangSplat, LangScene-X) under 32 views use a scene subset rather than the full validation set due to runtime constraints, which is understandable but slightly weakens the strength of the head-to-head claims in Table 2 relative to the full-set feed-forward comparisons in Table 1.
